name: Multi-container & init patterns
objective: CKAD › Application Design and Build + Observability. Drill EVERY pod-design corner harder than the exam: classic vs native sidecars, init ordering, all three probe types and handlers, lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown, full securityContext hardening, QoS classes, the Downward API, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Classic sidecar sharing an emptyDir
questions.teach:
A **sidecar** is a second container in the same pod. To share files, declare one `emptyDir` volume and mount it in **both** containers (at the same or different `mountPath`). The `emptyDir` is scratch space that lives and dies with the pod.

**Gotcha:** both containers must reference the **same volume name** — a typo gives each its own empty volume, so nothing is shared.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `sidecar-pod` in namespace `pod-design` with two containers sharing an `emptyDir`:
- `writer` (image `busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'while true; do date >> /data/out.log; sleep 1; done'`
- `reader` (image `busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'tail -F /data/out.log'`

Both mount the shared emptyDir at `/data`.
questions.hint: Define one `volumes: [{name: data, emptyDir: {}}]` and give BOTH containers `volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /data}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sidecar-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do date >> /data/out.log; sleep 1; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
  - name: reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /data/out.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
  volumes: [ { name: data, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: sidecar-pod: writer + reader share one emptyDir at /data

questions.eli5:
A **pod** is like a shared apartment, and the containers inside it are roommates. They share the same address (network) and can share a kitchen drawer for passing notes to each other. A **sidecar** is just a second roommate you add to help the first — here, one roommate (`writer`) keeps jotting the time into a shared notebook, and the other (`reader`) keeps reading it aloud.

The shared notebook is an **emptyDir** volume. "Empty" because it starts blank when the apartment is rented, and it's scratch paper — when the roommates move out (the pod is deleted), the notebook is thrown away. Nothing is saved permanently.

The trick that makes sharing work: you declare the notebook **once** for the apartment, then **both** roommates mount it at `/data`. Now when `writer` appends a line, `reader` sees it instantly, because it's literally the same notebook.

**Watch out for:**

- **Both containers must mount the SAME volume name.** If you typo the name, each roommate gets their own blank notebook and nothing is shared — the classic silent failure.
- **emptyDir is temporary.** It lives and dies with the pod; a container restart keeps it, but deleting the pod wipes it. Don't store anything you need to keep.
- **The mountPath can differ per container** (both use `/data` here, but they don't have to) — it's the volume *name* that must match.
- **They share the volume, but each has its own filesystem otherwise** — only the mounted path is common ground.
- **This "classic" sidecar is a plain second entry under `containers`** — it has no startup ordering guarantees relative to the main container.
questions.deepDive:
## Classic sidecar sharing an emptyDir — full rundown

### Mental model
A pod can hold **multiple containers** that share the pod's network namespace (same `localhost`/IP) and can share **volumes**. A **sidecar** is a helper container alongside the main one. To pass files between them, declare **one** `emptyDir` volume and mount it in **both** containers — it's shared scratch space that lives and dies with the pod.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do date >> /data/out.log; sleep 1; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
  - name: reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /data/out.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]      # same volume NAME
  volumes:
  - { name: data, emptyDir: {} }
```

### What containers in a pod share
| Shared | Not shared |
|---|---|
| Network (IP, ports, `localhost`) | Filesystem (except mounted volumes) |
| Volumes you mount in both | Process namespace (unless `shareProcessNamespace: true`) |
| Pod lifecycle, node | Container images / entrypoints |

### emptyDir basics
| Property | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Created | empty, when pod is assigned to a node |
| Lifetime | **as long as the pod** — survives container restarts, deleted with the pod |
| Backing | node disk by default; RAM with `emptyDir: { medium: Memory }` |
| Size cap | optional `sizeLimit` |
| Use | scratch space, inter-container file sharing, caches |

### Classic vs native sidecar
| | Classic sidecar | Native sidecar (1.29+) |
|---|---|---|
| Where | under `spec.containers` | under `spec.initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always` |
| Startup order | none guaranteed vs main | starts **before** main, ready first |
| Shutdown order | all together | native sidecar stops **after** main |
| Job completion | keeps Job pods alive | native sidecar won't block Job completion |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod sidecar-pod                      # 2/2 Running
kubectl -n pod-design logs sidecar-pod -c reader               # sees writer's lines
kubectl -n pod-design exec sidecar-pod -c reader -- cat /data/out.log
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Volume NAME must match in both mounts.** A mismatched name gives each container its own empty volume — nothing is shared, no error. The single most common sidecar bug.
- **emptyDir is ephemeral** — deleting the pod destroys the data; it's not persistence.
- **mountPath can differ** per container; the **name** is the binding, not the path.
- **One shared network** — containers reach each other on `localhost`; don't duplicate ports.
- **Logs are per-container** — use `-c <container>` with `logs`/`exec` in a multi-container pod, or you'll get an error / the default container.
- **`tail -F`** (capital F) follows by name through rotation/recreation; `-f` by descriptor.

### Quick reference
```yaml
containers:
- name: writer
  volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
- name: reader
  volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /data } ]
volumes: [ { name: data, emptyDir: {} } ]
```
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design logs sidecar-pod -c reader
```

questions.title: Init containers run to completion, in order
questions.teach:
**initContainers** (under `spec.initContainers`) run **sequentially, to completion** before any app container starts — each must exit 0 before the next begins. They run **top to bottom** in list order and share volumes with the app containers.

**Gotcha:** order is the list order — put `init-a` above `init-b`. A failing init container restarts and the app never starts (`Init:0/2`).
questions.prompt:
Create pod `init-pod` in `pod-design`:
- init container `init-a` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'echo a > /work/a'`
- then init container `init-b` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'echo b > /work/b'`
- main container `app` (`busybox:1.36`) runs `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`

All three mount the same `emptyDir` at `/work`, and the init containers must be ordered `init-a` then `init-b`.
questions.hint: `spec.initContainers` is an ordered list — put `init-a` before `init-b`. Share one emptyDir named e.g. `work` mounted at `/work` in all three containers.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: init-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init-a
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo a > /work/a"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  - name: init-b
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo b > /work/b"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  volumes: [ { name: work, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: init-pod: init-a then init-b (ordered) + app, sharing emptyDir at /work

questions.eli5:
Before the main show can start, sometimes you need setup crew to run first — unlock the doors, lay out the chairs, test the mic. **initContainers** are exactly that: little containers that run **before** your real app container, one after another, each finishing completely before the next begins. Only when all of them have succeeded does the main app start.

Think of it like a relay race where each runner must finish and pass the baton before the next runs. `init-a` runs first and must cross the finish line (exit cleanly). Then `init-b` runs. Then — and only then — your `app` container starts. The order is simply the order you list them in the YAML, top to bottom.

They can leave things behind for the app to use: here all three containers share the same scratch folder (`/work`), so the files `init-a` and `init-b` create are waiting there when `app` finally starts.

**Watch out for:**

- **Order = list order.** `init-a` before `init-b` in the YAML means `init-a` runs first. There's no priority field; position is everything.
- **Each init container must exit 0 to proceed.** If one fails, it **restarts** and the app never starts — you'll see status `Init:0/2` stuck.
- **They run one at a time, sequentially** — not in parallel. Slow init = slow pod start.
- **Share volumes to pass data forward** — same volume name mounted in init and app containers.
- **If an init container never succeeds, the pod hangs forever** — check with `kubectl logs <pod> -c init-a`.
- **These are one-shot:** they run, finish, and are done — unlike a native sidecar (next lesson) that keeps running.
questions.deepDive:
## Init containers — run to completion, in order

### Mental model
`spec.initContainers` run **sequentially, to completion, before any app container starts**. They execute **top-to-bottom in list order**; each must exit 0 before the next begins; all must succeed before `spec.containers` launch. They share the pod's volumes, so they can prepare state the app will consume.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init-a                 # runs FIRST
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo a > /work/a"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  - name: init-b                 # runs SECOND (after init-a exits 0)
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","echo b > /work/b"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  containers:
  - name: app                    # runs AFTER all init containers succeed
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ]
  volumes: [ { name: work, emptyDir: {} } ]
```

### Init vs app vs sidecar containers
| | initContainer | app container | native sidecar |
|---|---|---|---|
| Section | `initContainers` | `containers` | `initContainers` + `restartPolicy: Always` |
| Count | run once, exit | run continuously | run continuously |
| Order | sequential, before app | parallel, after init | before app, stays up |
| Failure | restarts; blocks app | per restartPolicy | restarts |

### Lifecycle & status
```
Init:0/2  → init-a running
Init:1/2  → init-a done, init-b running
Init:2/2  → inits done, app starting
Running   → app up
```
- A failing init container is retried per the pod's `restartPolicy` (default `Always` → keeps restarting) — the app **never** starts until it succeeds.
- Probes and lifecycle hooks don't apply to classic init containers.

### Common uses
- Wait for a dependency (`until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done`).
- Fetch/clone config or secrets into a shared `emptyDir`.
- Run schema migrations before the app boots.
- Set kernel/permissions on a shared volume.

### Debugging
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod init-pod                     # Init:x/2
kubectl -n pod-design logs init-pod -c init-a              # per-init logs
kubectl -n pod-design describe pod init-pod | sed -n '/Init Containers/,/Containers:/p'
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Order is list order** — no priority field. Put `init-a` above `init-b`.
- **Each must exit 0**; a non-zero exit restarts it and **blocks** the app (`Init:0/N`).
- **Sequential, not parallel** — total init time is the sum, which delays pod readiness.
- **Share a volume to pass data** — same volume name mounted in init + app.
- **Resource accounting:** the pod's effective request is the **max** of (largest single init request, sum of app requests) — init requests can raise scheduling requirements.
- A hung init (waiting on a dependency that never comes) leaves the pod stuck — check init logs first.

### Quick reference
```yaml
initContainers:
- { name: init-a, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sh","-c","echo a > /work/a"], volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ] }
- { name: init-b, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sh","-c","echo b > /work/b"], volumeMounts: [ { name: work, mountPath: /work } ] }
```
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design logs init-pod -c init-b
```

questions.title: Native sidecar (initContainer with restartPolicy: Always)
questions.teach:
A **native sidecar** (Kubernetes 1.29+) is an entry in `spec.initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always` set **on that container**. That one field makes it start before the app and stay running alongside it, instead of running once and exiting.

**Gotcha:** `restartPolicy: Always` goes on the init container itself, not on the pod spec.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `log-pod` in `pod-design` with a **native sidecar**:
- initContainer `logger` (`busybox:1.36`) with `restartPolicy: Always`, running `sh -c 'tail -F /var/log/app.log'`
- main container `app` (`busybox:1.36`) running `sh -c 'while true; do echo hi >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done'`

Share an `emptyDir` at `/var/log` in both.
questions.hint: Put `logger` under `spec.initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always` set ON that container. Share an emptyDir named e.g. `logs` at `/var/log`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: log-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: logger
    image: busybox:1.36
    restartPolicy: Always
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do echo hi >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  volumes: [ { name: logs, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: log-pod: native sidecar 'logger' (initContainer restartPolicy:Always) + app sharing /var/log

questions.eli5:
A regular init container is like a setup crew member who does one job and clocks out before the show. But some helpers need to **keep working the whole time** — like a sound engineer who sets up *and* stays at the mixing board all night. That's a **native sidecar**.

Here's the clever bit: a native sidecar lives in the `initContainers` list (so it starts *before* the main app, like other init crew), but you add one magic sticker to it — **`restartPolicy: Always`** — which tells Kubernetes: *"don't let this one finish and leave; start it first, then keep it running right alongside the app."* So your `logger` sidecar fires up, starts tailing the log file, and keeps tailing it the whole time the `app` is writing to it.

Why bother putting it in `initContainers` instead of just as a second normal container? Because this way Kubernetes **guarantees it's up and ready before the app starts**, and it **shuts down after** the app on termination — perfect for loggers and proxies that must be ready first and linger last.

**Watch out for:**

- **`restartPolicy: Always` goes ON the init container itself**, not on the pod spec. That one field is what turns an init container into a native sidecar.
- **It's a Kubernetes 1.29+ feature** — older clusters won't honor it (it'd run once and exit like a normal init container).
- **It still lives under `spec.initContainers`**, not `spec.containers` — that placement is what gives the start-before/stop-after ordering.
- **Unlike a classic init container, it does NOT need to exit** for the app to start — it starts, becomes ready, and the app proceeds while it keeps running.
- **Share volumes the same way** — same volume name mounted in both containers.
questions.deepDive:
## Native sidecar (initContainer + restartPolicy: Always)

### Mental model
A **native sidecar** (stable in Kubernetes **1.29+**) is an entry in `spec.initContainers` that carries **`restartPolicy: Always`** on that container. That single field changes its behaviour: instead of running once and exiting, it **starts before** the app containers, becomes ready, and **keeps running alongside** them — then shuts down **after** the main containers on termination. It gives you sidecar semantics with guaranteed startup/shutdown ordering.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: logger
    image: busybox:1.36
    restartPolicy: Always                 # ← makes it a NATIVE SIDECAR
    command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","while true; do echo hi >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
  volumes: [ { name: logs, emptyDir: {} } ]
```

### Classic sidecar vs native sidecar
| Aspect | Classic (`spec.containers`) | Native (`initContainers` + `restartPolicy: Always`) |
|---|---|---|
| Startup ordering | none vs app | **before** app; app waits for sidecar started/ready |
| Shutdown ordering | all together | sidecar stops **after** app |
| Job pods | sidecar keeps Job running forever | sidecar **won't block** Job completion |
| K8s version | any | **1.29+** (GA) |
| Probes | yes | yes (native sidecars support probes) |

### Why `initContainers` and not `containers`
- Placing it in `containers` (classic) gives no ordering guarantees and, in a **Job**, a never-exiting sidecar prevents the Job from ever completing.
- As a native sidecar it starts first, is ready before the app, lingers through app shutdown, and in Jobs is terminated once the main containers finish — solving the classic sidecar-in-a-Job problem.

### Field placement
| Field | Where |
|---|---|
| `restartPolicy: Always` (native sidecar) | **on the init container** |
| pod `restartPolicy` | `spec.restartPolicy` (pod-level; `Always`/`OnFailure`/`Never`) |

These are different fields at different levels — the per-container `restartPolicy` is only valid inside `initContainers`.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod log-pod                          # app Running, sidecar up
kubectl -n pod-design logs log-pod -c logger                   # sees app's lines
kubectl -n pod-design get pod log-pod \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.initContainers[0].restartPolicy}'; echo  # Always
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`restartPolicy: Always` goes on the container, not the pod** — the top exam trap here.
- **Must be under `spec.initContainers`** — moving it to `containers` makes it a classic sidecar (loses ordering).
- **Needs cluster ≥ 1.29** — on older versions the field is rejected or the container runs once and exits.
- **Does not need to exit** for the app to start (unlike classic init containers) — it only needs to start/become ready.
- **Supports probes** — a readiness probe on a native sidecar gates the app's start until the sidecar is ready.
- Share data via a common volume name, same as classic sidecars.

### Quick reference
```yaml
initContainers:
- name: logger
  image: busybox:1.36
  restartPolicy: Always
  command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log"]
  volumeMounts: [ { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log } ]
```
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod log-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.initContainers[0].restartPolicy}'
```
